description: We are an ambitious team of students passionate about AI, technology, science, and environmental research. Taking on NASA's Be an Earth Detective challenge, we aim to combine coding, data analysis, and creativity to uncover insights about our planet. We welcome teammates skilled in Python, AI/ML, data science, Earth science, satellite imagery, GIS, and UI/UX. Let's collaborate, innovate, and make an impact!
summary:
TrendTrace is a web app that turns NASA satellite data into plain-language answers to a simple question: is Earth really changing here? Users answer three quick questions about a topic, a place and their own curiosity. TrendTrace suggests relevant NASA variables, tests up to 22 years (2003-2024) of real data and reports what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is statistically real or just noise.

It addresses the challenge directly. Our engine removes the seasonal cycle, then applies a Hamed–Rao modified Mann–Kendall test, Theil–Sen slopes with uncertainty ranges, an OLS t-test and false-discovery control across many regions. It also estimates how many years a non-significant trend needs to become detectable. We use real data from Aqua and Terra MODIS, Aura OMI, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2 and NASA POWER, and any NASA Giovanni export can be uploaded for analysis.

It matters because it makes evidence accessible: students, journalists and planners can check claims about their own place, including honest verdicts like “no proven change.” Our findings include rising aerosol over the Indo-Gangetic Plain and Tamil Nadu and falling NO₂ over Los Angeles.
details:
What it does and how it works

TrendTrace helps anyone test whether something is really changing on Earth. Users answer three short questions (what, where, and their own question), and a transparent recommender suggests relevant NASA variables with plain-language definitions. One click then runs a trend test.

Our trendlib engine fetches real monthly NASA data (gaps stay gaps), removes the seasonal cycle, and applies a Hamed–Rao modified Mann–Kendall test, a Theil–Sen slope with its likely range, and an OLS t-test. Sensitivity runs produce an evidence label, and Benjamini–Hochberg control limits false positives across many regions. For non-significant trends, it estimates how many more years are needed to detect one. Users can also upload any NASA Giovanni export and download CSV or PDF reports.

Benefits and intended impact

Students, journalists, citizens and planners get statistically sound answers without writing code, with uncertainty and caveats on every result. “No proven change” is treated as a real answer, and disagreements between NASA products are shown rather than hidden. We want to turn “I heard it’s getting worse” into evidence. Our case studies include aerosol rising about 16% per decade over the Indo-Gangetic Plain and Tamil Nadu, Los Angeles NO₂ falling about 51% per decade, and Delhi NO₂ showing no proven all-year change.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA Giovanni (Aqua and Terra MODIS, Aura OMI, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2), NASA POWER, Natural Earth borders.
  • Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, our own trendlib statistics package, validated against SciPy and pymannkendall.
  • Frontend: plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript and three.js for the 3D globe.
  • Delivery: pytest (665 tests), GitHub Actions CI, Render hosting.
  • AI: an optional LLM that only rewords already-computed results, with automatic summaries as the fallback. AI coding tools (Codex, Claude) assisted development, with team review.

Creativity

A mission-themed 3D globe with scroll-driven “case files,” an astronaut guide named Trace, live warming stripes, and step-by-step demos. The distinctive part is honesty: we show cases where the answer is “no proven trend” or two NASA products disagree.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific rigor: seasonality, autocorrelation, missing data and multiple testing. AOD is column haze, not PM2.5, and a trend is not a cause.
  • Data integrity: nothing is filled or smoothed, and mock data is labelled and blocked in production.
  • AI safety: the LLM never computes numbers, and code rejects any changed figure or causal claim.
  • Accessibility: reduced-motion support, mobile scrolling, and a fallback when 3D graphics are unavailable.
  • Transparency: results are not an official NASA product.
